evaluated.name: AccrualDominatedGrowthOnly
evaluated.expression: MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RATIO(capx, at)), 0))
evaluated.hypothesis: Asset growth predicts low returns only in the state where accruals exceed real investment intensity; capex-dominated growth should not be penalized in the same way.
evaluated.reasoning: The indicator switches the asset-growth signal on exclusively for firms whose expansion is accounting-led (total accruals per asset above capex per asset), making the effect explicitly conditional rather than additive. If the mechanism is real, this conditional slope should be steeper than the unconditional asset-growth slope while leaving capex-heavy growers unpenalized.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: BoundedAccrualShareOfGrowth
evaluated.expression: RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), ADD(ABS(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), ABS(MA(capx, 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The composition of a firm's growth activity — the fraction contributed by non-cash working capital build-up rather than by real capital expenditure — predicts reversal, because paper growth unwinds while installed capacity does not.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the exploding accruals/capex ratio with a share that is mechanically bounded in [-1, 1], so small or zero capex can no longer generate extreme, sign-flipping cross-sectional ranks and the ordering is monotone in growth composition rather than in capex scarcity. Using a three-year capex average in the normalizer keeps the measure a statement about the firm's investment regime rather than one lumpy capital-budget year.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: BalanceSheetGrowthOutrunningWorkforce
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(COALESCE(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), 1), INDICATOR(SUB(GROWTH(at, 1), GROWTH(emp, 1)), 0))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accruals are most likely to be unproductive accounting expansion when the balance sheet grows faster than the workforce that must operate the assets; when headcount grows with assets, the same accruals reflect genuine scaling of operations.
evaluated.reasoning: Instead of subtracting a real-investment leg (whose own documented return relation runs the same negative direction and would cancel the accrual leg), employment growth enters purely as a state selector, so no leg is forced to carry a sign opposite to the established investment effect. It also removes the undefined growth-rate-of-working-capital problem by using an assets-scaled accrual level, and winsorizing bounds the continuous leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: UnstableAccrualsWithHeavyInvestment
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(VOL(COALESCE(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp), at)), 5)), IND_RANK(RATIO(MA(capx, 3), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Heavy capital spending is most likely to be value-destroying when the firm's accrual process is unstable, because volatile accruals indicate weak measurement of the profitability that is supposedly justifying the investment program.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the five-year accrual/capex difference, whose two legs predict returns with the same negative sign and therefore cancel, and instead pairs a second-moment accrual-quality state with an investment-intensity state so both legs push in the same direction and the product identifies the aggressive-investor/poor-measurement corner. It is not a restatement of net-operating-asset bloat because the accrual channel enters through its temporal instability, not its cumulated level.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: TotalAccrualShareOfGrowthActivity
evaluated.expression: RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(ABS(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp))), MA(capx, 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The fraction of a firm's total growth activity that is accrual accounting rather than real capital expenditure predicts reversal, and the broad accrual definition (earnings not backed by operating cash, including non-working-capital accruals) should capture more of the reversing component than the working-capital-only definition.
evaluated.reasoning: This holds the winning bounded-share architecture fixed and changes only the accrual numerator, so it directly tests whether total accruals or working-capital accruals is the right measure of "paper growth" in the composition ratio. The denominator adds strictly non-negative smoothed capex to the absolute accrual, so the signal stays bounded in [-1, 1] and cannot be hijacked by near-zero capex firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ExternallyFundedAccrualGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), at), 1), INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(sstk, DELTA(dltt, 1)), at), 0.05))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accrual-driven balance-sheet growth reverses hardest when it is financed with fresh external capital, because managers raising equity or debt have the strongest incentive and opportunity to inflate reported growth before the market can verify it.
evaluated.reasoning: The gate is a financing state (issuance above 5% of assets) rather than an accounting identity, so it selects the subsample where accruals are most likely to be strategic instead of mechanical — a mechanism absent from the archive. It follows the one conditional design that worked in gen 0 by gating a continuous, winsorized accrual variable rather than gating asset growth, avoiding a degenerate long leg of accrual-heavy shrinkers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWithDeceleratingCapex
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), 1), INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(capx, ppent), 1)), 0))
evaluated.hypothesis: Working-capital accrual build-up is a warning sign only when management is simultaneously cutting real investment intensity; expanding capex signals that the receivables and inventory build reflects genuinely anticipated demand.
evaluated.reasoning: This turns "growth quality deterioration" into a timing interaction — accounting growth continuing while real investment decelerates — which is a distinct state from the level-based conditioning already tested. Because the gate is a change in investment intensity rather than its level, the selected subsample is not simply low-capex firms, letting us separate investment *level* from investment *direction* as the conditioning variable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashFlowStatementAccrualShare
evaluated.expression: RATIO(NEG(ADD(recch, ADD(invch, apalch))), ADD(ABS(ADD(recch, ADD(invch, apalch))), MA(capx, 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Measuring the accounting-growth leg directly from the cash flow statement (increases in receivables and inventory net of payables) removes acquisition- and divestiture-driven balance-sheet noise, so the accrual-versus-capex composition share should be a cleaner and stronger predictor of reversal.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates one specific measurement choice inside the winning family: Hribar-Collins show balance-sheet accrual differences are contaminated by non-operating events, which mostly inflate the noise in the numerator. If coverage cost is modest and the t-stats improve, it tells us the winning signal is genuinely about operating working-capital growth rather than about balance-sheet mechanics.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: InvestmentUnderSofteningDepreciation
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(MA(capx, 3), ppegt)), INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, ppegt), 1)), 0))
evaluated.hypothesis: Heavy capital spending forecasts low returns specifically when the firm is simultaneously slowing its expense recognition — a falling depreciation rate on an unchanged capital base is an accounting choice that props up reported earnings while real capital is being over-accumulated.
evaluated.reasoning: This is no longer the net investment rate: the investment leg is industry-standardized capital intensity and the accrual leg enters as a *state* (declining depreciation rate on gross PP&E), so the signal tests whether the investment anomaly concentrates among firms whose earnings are also softened by expense deferral rather than restating capx minus dp. Standardizing the continuous leg places the gated-off firms at zero, i.e. in the middle of the sort, which avoids the degenerate long leg that killed the gen-0 indicator design.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CapexBeyondInternalCashFlow
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(MA(capx, 3), MA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), MA(at, 3)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital formation that exceeds internally generated operating cash must be funded by external capital or supported by accrual-inflated earnings, and such unfunded real investment reverses far more than investment paid for out of realized cash flow.
evaluated.reasoning: Instead of adding two anomaly ranks, this differences the two themes inside a single asset-scaled quantity — a multi-year investment/cash-flow gap — so the interaction is the funding shortfall itself rather than a blend of investment and profitability signals. Three-year averaging captures the sustained regime rather than one lumpy capital-budget year, and COALESCE substitutes funds from operations (ib plus dp) only where the cash flow statement does not exist, preserving coverage without changing the economics.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: InorganicGrowthShare
evaluated.expression: RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ABS(MA(aqc, 3))), ADD(ABS(ADD(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ABS(MA(aqc, 3)))), MA(capx, 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Acquisition spending belongs economically on the same side of the ledger as accruals rather than with organic capital expenditure, because purchased growth arrives as revalued balance-sheet items instead of internally built capacity, so the share of growth activity that is accrual-plus-acquisition should predict reversal more strongly than the accrual share alone.
evaluated.reasoning: This makes a testable economic claim about *what counts as productive investment*, which is the core question of the theme, rather than restating the winning ratio: if the alpha strengthens, acquisitions are accounting growth; if it weakens, only organic capex has the disciplining property. Acquisitions enter in absolute smoothed form so that divestiture-driven negative aqc values cannot flip the numerator's sign.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: UnexpensedSoftAssetGrowth
evaluated.expression: RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, ppent), che), 1), ADD(ABS(DELTA(SUB(SUB(at, ppent), che), 1)), MA(dp, 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Growth concentrated in non-cash, non-depreciable assets (receivables, inventory, intangibles, goodwill) escapes the income-statement discipline that depreciation imposes on real capital, so soft-asset expansion measured relative to the firm's expensing flow marks growth that must eventually be written off rather than depreciated.
evaluated.reasoning: The mechanism is new to the archive — expensing discipline rather than cash funding or investment direction — and depreciation is the natural cross-theme normalizer because it is the accounting rate at which real capital is consumed. Netting out cash prevents liquidity build-ups, which have the opposite return relation, from contaminating the soft-asset numerator, and the self-normalizing denominator keeps the measure bounded.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWhenCapexOutrunsCashFlow
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), at), 1), INDICATOR(SUB(MA(capx, 3), MA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), 0))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accruals are most misleading in firms whose capital spending already exceeds the cash their operations generate, because such firms have both the incentive to report growth they cannot fund and no cash cushion to absorb the reversal.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs two archive failures at once: it replaces the useless securities-issuance gate with a real investment-funding shortfall, and it converts the FF5-spanned capex-minus-cash-flow level into a conditioning state so the tradable spread comes from accrual dispersion inside the unfunded-investor subsample rather than from an investment factor tilt. The continuous leg is a winsorized accrual intensity, the one conditional structure that has produced reliable alpha in this archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsPerUnitRealCapitalFlow
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The right yardstick for accounting growth is the firm's total real capital flow — new investment plus capital consumption — so accruals per dollar of gross capital activity measure how much reported growth exists relative to the physical business actually being run.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates the normalizer choice: the denominator is strictly positive and economically meaningful (gross capital turnover) instead of the self-normalizing |accrual| term, which mechanically compresses large accruals toward ±1 and tilts the short leg toward asset-light firms. Comparing its alpha with the bounded-share winner tells us whether the winning signal works through growth *composition* or through the low-capex tilt embedded in its denominator.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ExpanderGrowthComposition
evaluated.expression: MUL(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(ABS(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp))), MA(capx, 3))), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0.05))
evaluated.hypothesis: The composition of growth should matter only for firms that are actually growing: among balance-sheet expanders, accrual-led expansion reverses while capex-led expansion does not, whereas for stagnant or shrinking firms the same ratio carries no growth-quality information.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the direct test of the theme's economic story — accrual-driven versus investment-driven *asset growth* — and it discriminates between two explanations of the archive winner: a genuine growth-composition effect versus a general accrual/asset-light effect that has nothing to do with expansion. Because the share is bounded in [-1, 1], the gated-off firms sit at zero in the middle of the sort rather than degrading a tail leg, the flaw that sank the gen-0 gated asset-growth signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualDominanceYearCount
evaluated.expression: TS_SUM(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), at), RATIO(capx, at)), 0), 5)
evaluated.hypothesis: What predicts reversal is not the size of this year's accrual-led growth but how habitually a firm has expanded through accruals rather than capital expenditure; a firm that has been accrual-dominated in four or five of the last five years is running a chronically soft growth model, while one isolated accrual-dominated year is a transitory event.
evaluated.reasoning: This discards magnitude entirely and measures only the frequency of the cross-theme dominance state, so it answers the persistence-versus-event question with information that is genuinely orthogonal to the archive winner's level rather than by smoothing it. It also repairs the gen-0 failure of AccrualDominatedGrowthOnly, where the same dominance condition was multiplied by contemporaneous asset growth and produced a degenerate zero mass point; here every firm receives an informative integer score from zero to five.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WCAccrualPerRealCapitalFlow
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The reversing component of accounting growth is the working-capital build-up itself, measured against the scale of the firm's real capital activity; if this alone reproduces the archive's alpha, the accrual anomaly is about operating working capital rather than about depreciation policy.
evaluated.reasoning: This completes the missing cell of the 2x2 design grid (working-capital versus total accrual numerator, crossed with self-normalized versus gross-capital-flow denominator) and is the only clean way to attribute the −5% alpha of the two leading signals to a specific accrual component. Winsorizing guards the tail where capx+dp is small for asset-light firms, the instability the critic flagged.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: GrowthQualityDeterioration
evaluated.expression: DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(ABS(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp))), MA(capx, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The market prices a firm's established growth model, so what surprises it is a shift in composition — a firm that was expanding through capital expenditure and is now expanding through accruals is deteriorating in a way not yet reflected in its valuation.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a change rather than a smoothing of the level, so it carries information the archive winner cannot contain: it is near zero for chronically accrual-led firms already known to the market and extreme only for firms whose growth quality just flipped. The parent ratio is bounded in [-1,1], so its first difference is also bounded and cannot produce the ratio-explosion pathology seen in earlier designs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: UnamortizedIntangibleBuildup
evaluated.expression: RATIO(DELTA(intan, 1), ADD(ABS(DELTA(intan, 1)), MA(dp, 3)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Intangible and goodwill balances added to the books are capital that has been recognized but is largely shielded from systematic expensing, so firms whose intangible base grows large relative to their total amortization and depreciation flow are carrying asset values that must eventually be resolved through impairment rather than through orderly cost recognition.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the incorrect capx-minus-dp "decomposition" claim and instead tests a specific accounting-versus-real asset distinction: the growth in the least verifiable asset category measured against the firm's actual expensing capacity. It is not the net investment rate — the numerator contains no capital expenditure at all — and the impairment channel it targets is absent from the archive, where acquisitions entered only through aqc spending flows.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SustainedAccrualLedGrowth
evaluated.expression: MIN(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(ABS(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp))), MA(capx, 3))), LAG(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(ABS(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp))), MA(capx, 3))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Only growth that has been accrual-led in consecutive years reflects a genuine accounting-driven growth model; a single accrual-heavy year can be an ordinary demand or contract-timing event that the market correctly ignores, so requiring the composition to be soft in both the current and prior year should isolate the reversing population.
evaluated.reasoning: Taking the minimum of the composition share and its own lag is a continuous logical AND — it scores high only when both years are accrual-dominated — which answers the persistence question that the discrete AccrualDominanceYearCount could not, since that signal's coarse integer values produced nan portfolio statistics. Unlike a moving average, MIN does not let one strongly capex-led year offset an extreme accrual year, so it targets sustained softness rather than an averaged level.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualVersusLaborExpansion
evaluated.expression: RATIO(WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), at), 1), ADD(ABS(WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), at), 1)), ABS(GROWTH(emp, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Labor is the investment input that cannot be booked without being paid for, so a firm expanding its balance sheet through accruals while its workforce is flat is growing in a way no real operating commitment corroborates, whereas accruals accompanied by hiring reflect genuine scaling of the business.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the inventory numerator, which was a rediscovery of a published anomaly, with a real-investment yardstick that is orthogonal to capital spending and has been used in this archive only inside a failed binary gate. Both legs are dimensionless rates (accruals per asset and employment growth), so the self-normalized share is bounded in [-1,1] and comparable across capital-intensive and labor-intensive firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsAgainstDecliningCashGeneration
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), DELTA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 1)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Accounting growth is most likely to reverse when the cash engine behind it is already weakening: high accruals combined with a year-over-year fall in operating cash flow means reported expansion is being sustained precisely as its cash validation disappears.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the change in taxes payable, the change in operating cash flow is the same order of magnitude as total accruals, so this is a material perturbation that adds a dynamic cash-validation dimension rather than a negligible relabeling of the parent signal. It keeps the real-capital-activity denominator that already produces reliable alpha, so any improvement is attributable to the cash-deterioration term in the numerator.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SustainedCashUnbackedAccruals
evaluated.expression: MIN(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), DELTA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 1)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), LAG(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), DELTA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 1)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Reversal is concentrated in firms whose growth has been both cash-unbacked and persistently so: a single year of accruals outrunning cash generation can be contract timing, but two consecutive years identify a growth model that only exists on the income statement.
evaluated.reasoning: This stacks the archive's two independently validated improvements — the cash-deterioration numerator that produced the strongest alpha t-stat (−5.46) and the MIN-with-lag persistence operator that produced the best Sharpe (−0.43) — which are structurally orthogonal, one acting on measurement and the other on timing. MIN keeps the construction continuous, avoiding the coarse-integer failure that made the persistence-count signal untradeable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: TrendCashUnbackedAccruals
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for the credibility of accrual-led growth is the direction of the cash engine over the investment cycle, not one noisy fiscal year, so a multi-year decline in operating cash generation should be a sharper disconfirmation of reported growth than a single-year drop.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates the temporal form of the cash-validation term inside the current best signal, replacing a one-year difference with a three-year slope while holding numerator scale, deflator and winsorization fixed. Because year-to-year operating cash flow is volatile, the trend version should raise the slope reliability if the mechanism is a genuine cash-engine deterioration rather than a one-off accrual accounting artifact.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualsWhileCashBufferDrains
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), DELTA(che, 1)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Accrual-led growth is most dangerous when the liquidity stock that would absorb its reversal is simultaneously shrinking; a firm booking receivables and inventory while its cash balance falls has no buffer against the working-capital unwind.
evaluated.reasoning: This substitutes a stock-based validation (change in the cash balance) for the flow-based one (change in operating cash flow) that currently works, testing whether the mechanism is about the cash engine or about the liquidity cushion — economically distinct sources of reversal risk with very different implications for refinement. It keeps every other element of the leading design fixed, so the comparison is clean.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: OwnHistoryExtremeOfPaperGrowth
evaluated.expression: TS_RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), DELTA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 1)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), 5)
evaluated.hypothesis: Investors anchor on a firm's established growth model, so mispricing arises when cash-unbacked accrual growth reaches an unusual level *for that firm*, regardless of where the firm sits in the cross-section of capital intensity.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has tested the level (strong), the one-year change (weak, t −1.6) and two-year persistence (strong), but never the firm's position within its own five-year distribution, which is the remaining temporal form and is naturally bounded in [0,1] — ideal for stable quantile sorts. A strong result would mean the effect is a within-firm surprise; a weak one would confirm that the cross-sectional level, not the firm-relative deviation, is what the market misprices.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NonCashCapitalGrowth
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ppegt, 1), capx), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Gross property, plant and equipment can rise for reasons that never involved a dollar of capital spending — acquired asset step-ups, capitalized overhead and interest, revaluations and consolidations — and this non-cash portion of capital growth is accounting growth wearing the clothes of productive investment, so it should reverse like an accrual while capex-backed capacity growth should not.
evaluated.reasoning: This moves the accounting-versus-real distinction inside the capital account itself, comparing the balance-sheet capital increase with the cash-flow-statement capital outlay, a construct no archive signal has touched and one that is not a decomposition of Sloan accruals. The deflator is the validated gross-capital-flow scale so the only new element is the numerator, and winsorization contains the retirement-driven negative tail.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WorstOfTwoSoftGrowthChannels
evaluated.expression: MAX(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(ABS(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp))), MA(capx, 3))), RATIO(DELTA(intan, 1), ADD(ABS(DELTA(intan, 1)), MA(dp, 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Growth quality is compromised if expansion is soft on *either* dimension — cash-unbacked working-capital accruals or a build-up of intangible assets shielded from amortization — so the firms that should be shorted are those failing at least one test, while the long leg should contain only firms whose growth is clean on both.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a union rather than an intersection of two channels that the archive has separately validated in different metrics (the accrual share carried the alpha at t −5.0, the intangible build-up carried the slope at t −3.9), and taking the maximum of two ratios already bounded in [-1,1] keeps the composite bounded and comparable without any deflator change. It replaces the rejected rescaling with a structural aggregation hypothesis whose failure would be equally informative: it would say the two channels are substitutes, not complements, and that intangible build-up simply does not reverse in tradable form.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DualValidationSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), DELTA(che, 1)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Reported growth can be disconfirmed by two independent cash facts — a deteriorating operating cash flow trend and a falling cash balance — and a firm failing both tests has neither an engine nor a buffer, so combining the flow and stock validations should identify the most fragile accounting growth.
evaluated.reasoning: The two validation terms have complementary empirical profiles in the archive (the trend version carries the slope at −4.01, the cash-buffer version carries the alpha t at −6.64 with a weak slope of −1.51), which is exactly the pattern that motivates additive combination rather than choosing between them. All three components are dollar flows on the same scale and share the validated deflator, so no rescaling artifact is introduced.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: GrowthCompositionInstability
evaluated.expression: VOL(RATIO(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), ADD(ABS(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp))), MA(capx, 3))), 5)
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that keeps switching between accrual-led and capex-led expansion has no stable growth process, and such instability signals weak accounting discipline and poor project selection, so the volatility of growth composition should predict low returns independently of its level.
evaluated.reasoning: The one second-moment idea in the archive failed, but it failed as a rank product with capital intensity (fmb +0.40), never as a clean volatility of the composition ratio itself, and the ratio is bounded in [-1,1] so its volatility is well scaled and cannot be driven by denominator explosions. This is the only proposal in the batch whose information is not a transformation of the current level signal, so it also serves as an orthogonality probe for the family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AgedCapitalSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), MUL(ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3)), RATIO(ppent, ppegt))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The same dollar of cash-unbacked accrual growth is far more dangerous in a firm whose productive base is already largely depreciated, because such a firm faces an imminent replacement bill it is not funding while it books soft revenue; scaling the deflator by the undepreciated fraction of the capital stock makes the signal larger exactly for those aged-asset firms.
evaluated.reasoning: Asset age (net over gross PP&E) is a new interaction dimension for this archive — every prior signal treated capital only through flows — and it enters as a strictly positive multiplier bounded between zero and one, so it rescales rather than re-signs the validated numerator and cannot create a sign conflict. It is not a recombination of two tested designs: the hypothesis is that vintage of installed capital moderates the reversal of accounting growth.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WorkingCapitalIntensityDrift
evaluated.expression: TREND(RATIO(wcap, ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 3)
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose stock of working capital keeps rising relative to the scale of its physical operations is accumulating an overhang of unconverted operating assets, and this multi-year drift in accounting intensity — not any single year's accrual flow — measures how far reported growth has detached from the real business.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive signal so far measures a one-year accrual *flow*; this measures the drift of a working-capital *stock* normalized by real capital activity, a different measurement basis whose information is cumulative rather than incremental and which cannot be obtained by reweighting the existing numerator. It replaces the rejected parameter tweak with a construct that is economically distinct while retaining the deflator that has repeatedly delivered tradable alpha.

evaluated.name: DebtFundedSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(DELTA(dlc, 1), DELTA(dltt, 1))), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-unbacked accounting growth financed by new borrowing is the most fragile configuration, because the working-capital unwind arrives alongside a refinancing requirement, whereas the same accruals in a firm repaying debt are being absorbed by a strengthening balance sheet.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's two financing-conditioning attempts failed as binary gates (fmb +0.42 and +0.48) because gated-off firms piled up at zero; this puts the same economics into the numerator continuously and at a dollar magnitude comparable to the accrual term, which is the construction style that has consistently produced alpha here. Debt growth and accrual softness both predict low returns, so the legs reinforce rather than offset.

evaluated.name: SoftGrowthWithDepreciationRelief
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), MUL(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, ppegt), 1)), ppegt)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms supporting reported growth with accruals often reach for a second accounting lever — slowing the rate at which they depreciate an unchanged capital base — and the dollars of expense thereby avoided belong in the same soft-growth numerator as the cash-unbacked accrual itself.
evaluated.reasoning: The added term is the depreciation-rate deceleration converted to dollars by multiplying through by the gross capital stock, so it is materially sized rather than a negligible perturbation, and it does not double-count the deflator: it depends on the *change in the depreciation rate*, not on the level of capex. This repairs the earlier depreciation-policy signal that produced a wrong-signed alpha (+2.5) when used as a binary gate on capital intensity, by moving the same accounting-choice idea inside the validated continuous numerator.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DepreciationReliefDollars
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(MUL(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, ppegt), 1)), ppegt), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Extending assumed asset lives is an accrual choice that manufactures earnings without any operating event, so the dollars of depreciation a firm avoided by slowing its expensing rate should predict low returns on their own, independent of working-capital accruals.
evaluated.reasoning: The depreciation-relief term was added inside a composite last generation and improved both metrics, but we cannot tell whether it contributed independent information or merely re-weighted the accrual leg; this isolation test settles the attribution and, if strong, identifies a standalone lever for the final generations. It is a genuine investment-x-accruals object — a depreciation policy change measured against the gross capital stock and scaled by real capital activity — not a restatement of the investment rate, since it depends on the change in the expensing rate rather than on capex.

evaluated.name: CumulativeAccrualBloatCashValidated
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(TS_SUM(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), 3), SUB(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), LAG(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3))), ADD(TS_SUM(capx, 3), TS_SUM(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Accounting growth accumulates: three years of accruals that have not been ratified by any three-year improvement in operating cash generation represent a stock of unconverted reported growth, and that stock should reverse more reliably than a single year's accrual flow.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive signal has varied the *cash-validation* horizon while holding the accrual leg at one year; this is the untested dimension, and it is not a net-operating-asset rediscovery because the cumulative accrual is explicitly netted against the cumulative cash-flow improvement over the same window. Numerator and deflator are both three-year sums, so the ratio remains dimensionless and directly comparable to the one-year members of the family.

evaluated.name: LeveragedSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cash-unbacked accounting growth becomes a repricing event only when creditors are involved: a levered firm whose accruals reverse faces covenant pressure and forced retrenchment, while an unlevered firm simply absorbs the unwind, so the return consequence of soft growth should scale with the stock of interest-bearing debt.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a moderating-state hypothesis about *who bears the reversal*, not a rescaling of the softness measure — the debt-to-assets multiplier is a positive bounded weight, so unlevered firms are pushed to the middle of the sort rather than into a tail. It is distinct from the archive's DebtFundedSoftGrowth, which added debt *issuance flows* to the numerator and weakened the alpha; here leverage never enters the definition of softness, only its consequence.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ReversibleAssetShareSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), RATIO(SUB(act, che), at))
evaluated.hypothesis: The damage from soft growth depends on how much of the balance sheet consists of assets that must still convert into cash; a firm whose assets are mostly receivables and inventory has a large pool exposed to write-down, whereas the same accrual in a plant-heavy firm affects a small corner of the balance sheet.
evaluated.reasoning: The moderator is the *quantity at risk of reversal* — the non-cash operating current asset share — which is an economic amplification channel, unlike adding cash to the deflator, which merely retilts the same ranking toward cash-poor firms. It also sharpens the theme's core distinction: accounting growth is dangerous in proportion to how much of the firm is accounting assets rather than productive capital.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SoftGrowthWithRealRetrenchment
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), SUB(MA(capx, 3), capx)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Management reveals its private view when it accrues revenue in the reported numbers while quietly cutting capital spending below its own recent run rate; the dollars of investment withheld relative to the firm's own norm are a real-side confirmation that the reported growth is not expected to continue.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the magnitude-inconsistent cash-flow *level* benchmark with a term measured against the firm's own investment norm, so it is a deviation rather than a level and does not contradict the investment anomaly — low-capex firms are not penalized, only firms cutting capex relative to their own recent spending. The archive supports the channel: conditioning on decelerating capital intensity produced a −3.4% alpha at t −3.42 even in the crude binary form that discarded magnitude.

evaluated.name: ExpansionWeightedSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), IND_RANK(GROWTH(at, 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The theme's central claim is about the composition of *growth*, so the softness of reported expansion should matter most for firms that are actually expanding their balance sheets, and progressively less for stable or contracting firms whose reported growth carries no valuation premium to unwind.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive tested this idea only as a hard 5%-asset-growth indicator, which produced a strong alpha (−4.1%, t −4.76) but a diluted slope (−1.63) precisely because two thirds of firms were collapsed onto zero; replacing the gate with a continuous within-industry growth rank preserves ordering information for every firm while retaining the economic weighting. It abandons the dollar-summing "lever count" framing entirely and instead tests a single, clean moderation hypothesis.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SoftGrowthPerReversibleBase
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(SUB(act, che), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3)))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The right normalization for cash-unbacked growth is the total base that either produces cash or must still convert into it: adding the stock of non-cash operating current assets to real capital activity measures the annual paper growth as a rate on the whole convertible-plus-productive base.
evaluated.reasoning: The multiplicative moderator and this deflator embed the same economics with opposite mechanics — one amplifies exposure, the other divides by it — so evaluating both settles whether reversal risk scales with the exposed pool (moderator wins) or is diluted by it (deflator wins), which no archive result can currently distinguish. The larger, strictly positive denominator should also stabilize the thin tails that capx+dp leaves for asset-light firms without introducing the leverage-style factor tilt that destroyed alpha in gen 6.

evaluated.name: InventoryExposureSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), RATIO(invt, at))
evaluated.hypothesis: Within the pool of reversible operating assets, inventory is the component whose reversal is physically unavoidable — unsold goods must be marked down or written off — whereas receivables can often be collected, so inventory intensity should be the active part of the exposure moderator.
evaluated.reasoning: This decomposes the moderator that delivered the archive's best slope, which is the natural next diagnostic: if inventory intensity alone reproduces the −6 slope, the mechanism is production-and-markdown risk; if it does not, the moderator is about the breadth of the operating asset base rather than any single component. The weight remains a positive share bounded in [0,1], so the construction inherits the numerical stability of the parent.

evaluated.name: CapitalProductivityAdjustedSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), MUL(DELTA(RATIO(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), ppent), 1), ppent)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: What disconfirms accrual-led growth is not a smaller cash flow but a falling cash return on installed capital: converting the change in cash flow per dollar of net PP&E back into dollars isolates deteriorating productivity of the existing asset base from the mere scale of cash generation.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new validation construct rather than another horizon for the same term — it uses the same rate-times-stock arithmetic that made the depreciation-relief lever work, applied to cash productivity instead of expensing policy, so firms that grow cash flow only by adding capital receive no credit. It should sharpen the slope relative to TREND-based validation if the mechanism is unproductive investment paired with soft accounting, and it keeps every other element of the leading design fixed.

evaluated.name: OrganicNonCashCapitalGrowth
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(ppegt, 1), capx), ABS(MA(aqc, 3))), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Gross capital that appears on the balance sheet without corresponding cash outlay is accounting capital growth, but the archive's contradictory result for this construct (slope −4.57 alongside a positive portfolio alpha) should be traceable to acquisition step-ups populating one tail; removing acquisition spending should leave a cleanly signed measure of capitalized-cost and revaluation growth.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the one unresolved contradiction in the archive, and resolving it matters because it is the only place where the balance-sheet-versus-cash distinction is applied to the capital account rather than to working capital. If purging acquisitions aligns the portfolio evidence with the cross-sectional slope, the capital-account channel becomes usable in the final generation; if the conflict persists, we can conclude the extremes are impairment-driven and abandon the channel permanently.

evaluated.name: PerLeverNormalizedSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), SUB(act, che)), NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, ppegt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Each accounting lever should be judged against the base it distorts: working-capital softness against the pool of operating current assets that must convert to cash, and expensing relief against the capital stock whose life has been stretched — so a firm is soft if it scores highly on the lever relevant to its own asset structure, not on a single common deflator.
evaluated.reasoning: This fixes the inconsistency the critic identified: instead of multiplying the whole composite by a working-capital weight that shrinks plant-heavy firms toward zero, each lever is normalized by its own base so working-capital-heavy and plant-heavy firms can each register softness on the dimension that applies to them. Every prior composite in the archive summed dollars under one deflator, which mechanically lets the largest term dominate; ranking the two incomparably scaled rates before combining is the structurally correct way to weight them equally and is new to this search.

evaluated.name: SlowConversionSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, che), ADD(ABS(MA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3)))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: What amplifies the reversal is not merely how large the pool of unconverted operating assets is, but how slowly that pool turns into cash: a firm needing several years of operating cash flow to work off its receivables and inventory has a long, uncertain conversion horizon over which soft growth can unwind.
evaluated.reasoning: The moderator is a conversion-horizon measure — the exposed asset pool expressed in units of the firm's annual cash-and-capital activity — which is an economically different quantity from the exposure *share* of assets tested in gen 6, since two firms with identical operating-asset shares can differ greatly in how fast those assets cycle. The denominator is strictly positive and includes both cash generation and capital activity, so the multiplier cannot explode for low-cash-flow firms, and winsorization caps the remaining tail.

evaluated.name: HorizonModeratedDepreciationReliefSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), MUL(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, ppegt), 1)), ppegt)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(act, che), ADD(ABS(MA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3)))), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Softness registered on either lever — working-capital accruals unbacked by cash or expense deferral through slower depreciation — should be amplified by how long the firm's unconverted operating assets take to turn into cash, because a long conversion horizon is the window over which any form of reported softness must unwind.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the reversible-asset *share* moderator that was rightly criticised for zeroing plant-heavy firms, the conversion-horizon moderator stays substantial for capital-intensive firms precisely because their cash flow is small relative to their receivable and inventory pool, so the depreciation lever's information is preserved rather than annihilated. The two ingredients are the archive's best slope moderator (−5.55) and its best alpha numerator (−5.9%, t −6.29), and the economic claim — horizon governs how long any lever's distortion persists — is consistent for both.

evaluated.name: HorizonModeratedCumulativeBloat

evaluated.hypothesis: A three-year stock of accruals unratified by any three-year cash improvement is the accumulated overhang, and the conversion horizon tells us how slowly that overhang can be worked off, so the two should compound: a large overhang in a slow-converting business is the most reversal-prone configuration.
evaluated.reasoning: The cumulative base carries the archive's joint best alpha and Sharpe (−6.0%, −0.442) and the horizon moderator carries its best slope, and pairing them tests whether the moderator's amplification is horizon-specific rather than tied to the one-year accrual flow. Comparing this with signal 1 identifies which numerator horizon the moderator complements, which is the key design decision for the final generation.

evaluated.hypothesis: The sharpest disconfirmation of reported growth is the distance between the cash the business once generated and what it generates now: a firm accruing revenue while operating cash flow sits far below its own five-year peak is defending a valuation its cash engine no longer supports.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new validation construct — a drawdown from the firm's own cash-flow high-water mark rather than a slope, a change or a level — and it is strictly non-negative, so it cannot offset the accrual term the way a trend with either sign can, which may explain why trend-based validation trades slope against alpha in the archive. It keeps the validated deflator unchanged so the comparison isolates the drawdown construct.

evaluated.name: WeakCashGenerationWeightedSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), RATIO(ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3)), ADD(ABS(MA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The conversion-horizon moderator may be working not through the size of the exposed asset pool but through its denominator: firms whose capital activity dwarfs their operating cash generation have no internal means of absorbing an accrual reversal, and that cash-generation weakness alone may drive the amplification.

If it reproduces the −5.5 slope, the final generation should build on cash-generation weakness; if it does not, the exposed pool is the essential ingredient.

evaluated.name: ExcessUnconvertedOperatingAssets
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), SUB(SUB(act, che), MUL(MA(RATIO(SUB(act, che), ADD(ABS(MA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3)))), 3), ADD(ABS(MA(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3)))))), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Beyond this year's accrual flow, a firm can be carrying a stock of operating assets far larger than its own normal conversion horizon implies; those excess unconverted dollars are past reported growth that never became cash and must still be written down or worked off.

The overhang is materially sized relative to the accrual flow and shares the validated deflator, so any improvement is attributable to the new term rather than to scaling.

evaluated.name: TradeCreditFundedSoftGrowth
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(SUB(ib, oancf), SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), dp)), TREND(COALESCE(oancf, ADD(ib, dp)), 3)), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3))), 1), RATIO(SUB(lct, dlc), ADD(SUB(act, che), ADD(MA(capx, 3), MA(dp, 3)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Soft growth is most dangerous when the operating base behind it is funded by suppliers rather than by the firm's own resources, because trade credit is the fastest funding source to be withdrawn once payment problems appear, forcing an abrupt liquidation of receivables and inventory.

evaluated.name: DrawdownAndDepreciationSoftGrowth

evaluated.hypothesis: The clearest case of accounting rather than productive growth is a firm accruing revenue while its operating cash flow sits far below its own historical peak and it is simultaneously slowing depreciation to protect reported earnings.

evaluated.name: PeakCapitalProductivityDrawdownSoftGrowth

evaluated.hypothesis: The decisive disconfirmation of accrual-led growth is a fall in the cash a firm extracts per dollar of installed capital relative to the best that capital ever produced; expressed in dollars, that productivity drawdown measures how much reported growth the existing asset base can no longer support.
evaluated.reasoning: This fuses the two constructs the critic rated highest — rate-times-stock conversion of an efficiency change into dollars, and the non-negative high-water-mark drawdown — into a single validation term that penalizes firms whose cash flow grew only because capital grew, which neither the cash-level trend nor the raw drawdown can do. It is the batch's genuinely new mechanism and, if it beats the raw drawdown, it identifies capital productivity rather than cash scale as the economic content of the validation term.
