critic_notes.rationale: This is an equal-weighted rank blend of two of the most heavily documented anomalies (Cooper-Gulen-Schill asset growth and Sloan/Richardson balance-sheet accruals) that are themselves strongly correlated and both largely spanned by the FF5 CMA factor, so it is a rediscovery/repackaging rather than a genuine interaction, and SUMRANK enforces additivity precisely where the hypothesis claims conditionality.

The composition idea (accounting growth per dollar of real investment) is reasonably fresh, but the construction is fragile — winsorizing the denominator at 1% still leaves near-zero and negative-accrual cases that make the ratio explode and flip sign non-monotonically, so cross-sectional ranks will be driven by low-capex firms rather than by growth composition; a bounded form (e.g., accruals minus capex, both scaled by assets, or a rank difference) would test the same economics far more cleanly.

The conditional design is internally consistent and is a legitimate sharpening test of whether the asset-growth effect concentrates in accrual-led expanders, but it creates a large mass point at exactly zero (all capex-dominated firms) that will dominate middle quantiles and make the long leg consist of accrual-dominated *shrinkers* rather than the "unpenalized" firms the hypothesis describes, and the use of oancf restricts coverage to post-1988.

Two defects: the growth rate of non-cash working capital is undefined/sign-flipping for the many firms with near-zero or negative working capital, and the positive expected sign requires the long leg to be high gross-PP&E-growth firms, which the well-established investment/CMA anomaly says underperform — so the stated sign fights the natural direction of the dominant leg.

The first leg is essentially the published inventory-growth anomaly (Thomas-Zhang, Belo-Lin), and the second leg is deliberately sign-flipped investment growth, so the composite goes long high-PP&E-growth firms in direct opposition to the documented investment effect — the two legs are likely to offset rather than reinforce, and the "capacity" conditioning would be better expressed as an interaction than as an additive rank sum.

Cumulating accruals over five years is close to a re-derivation of the net-operating-assets/balance-sheet-bloat anomaly (Hirshleifer et al.), and the negatively signed capex leg contradicts Fairfield-Whisenant-Yohn's finding that long-term operating-asset growth predicts returns with the same negative sign as accruals, so the differencing likely cancels signal instead of isolating composition.

A legitimate single-input measurement swap (total cash-flow-based accruals vs. working-capital accruals) inside the archive's best-performing bounded-share architecture with correct sign and no scaling pathologies, but it is incremental rather than a new mechanism and overlaps substantially with the CashFlowStatementAccrualShare proposal in the same batch.

(capx − dp)/ppegt is essentially the net investment rate in PP&E — a direct restatement of the published investment/asset-growth anomaly — and the "under-depreciation as accounting choice" story is unsupported since low dp relative to capx mostly reflects a young asset base, so this is a single trivial ratio rather than a cross-theme interaction.

The financing-state gate is economically coherent and sign-consistent, though it edges toward the published result that the accrual anomaly concentrates in external-financing firms, and the hard 5%-of-assets indicator leaves a large mass point at exactly zero that will make the sorted portfolio legs lumpy and composition-unstable.

Conditioning on the *direction* of investment intensity rather than its level is a genuinely different state variable from anything in the archive, the indicator's sign correctly matches the stated hypothesis, and the winsorized continuous accrual leg avoids a degenerate long side — the main risk is noise in Δ(capx/ppent) for asset-light firms.

The Compustat sign conventions work out correctly (NEG of recch+invch+apalch does recover ΔAR+ΔINV−ΔAP) and the Hribar–Collins motivation is the right diagnostic for whether the winning signal is about operating working capital, but it is a measurement refinement of an existing archive signal and cash-flow-statement items will materially cut coverage.

This is a plain additive rank blend of two already-known anomaly legs (investment growth and cash-flow/profitability growth) with no conditioning or interaction, so it rediscovers the standard investment-times-profitability combination and tells you nothing about the cross-theme mechanism the archive is probing.

This is a three-year moving average of the archive's existing winner (TotalAccrualShareOfGrowthActivity) with numerator, denominator and bounding unchanged — a cosmetic smoothing variant whose denominator already contains a 3-year capex average, so the incremental information content is minimal and the "persistence vs. event" question could be answered more cleanly by a persistence indicator or by regressing on the lagged level.

Reclassifying acquisition spending from the "real investment" side to the "accounting growth" side is a substantive, falsifiable economic claim about what counts as productive growth rather than a re-parameterization, and the ABS-and-smooth treatment of aqc sensibly guards against sign flips from divestitures — though the result will need care to separate a genuine composition effect from a straight rediscovery of the well-known acquirer-underperformance anomaly.

The expensing-discipline mechanism and the depreciation-flow normalizer are new to this archive and internally consistent (rising soft assets → signal toward +1 → predicted low returns, matching the negative sign), but the numerator is close to a re-derivation of published growth-in-net-operating-assets / soft-assets-ratio measures, so the marginal contribution rests entirely on whether the dp-based denominator adds anything beyond scaling by assets.

Replacing the failed securities-issuance gate with an investment-funding shortfall is a defensible diagnosis-driven repair and the conditioning variable had the archive's strongest FMB slope, but the design is structurally identical to ExternallyFundedAccrualGrowth (winsorized accrual level × binary gate), so the same problem of gated-off firms piling at zero and diluting the tails may recur.

The proposal correctly identifies a real confound — the self-normalizing |accrual| denominator mechanically compresses extremes and tilts the short leg toward asset-light firms — and tests it with a strictly positive, economically interpretable gross-capital-flow denominator, though capx+dp approaches zero for asset-light firms and winsorization alone may not tame the resulting tail instability.

Gating the winning composition share on actual balance-sheet expansion is the right discriminating test between a growth-composition story and a generic accrual/asset-light tilt, and the argument that zeroed-out firms land mid-sort in a [-1,1]-bounded signal is correct, but the gen-0 AccrualDominatedGrowthOnly result suggests such asset-growth gates have destroyed rather than sharpened signal here, so the informational value lies mainly in a negative result.

A coherent and internally consistent attribution test that fills the genuine missing cell of the numerator×denominator grid, though it is ultimately a rescaled working-capital accrual (Sloan) measure and likely to be highly correlated with the archive's existing AccrualsPerUnitRealCapitalFlow, so its value is diagnostic rather than novel.

(capx−dp)/(capx+dp) is a bounded monotone transform of capx/dp, i.e. a direct restatement of the well-known net-investment/capital-investment anomaly, and the stated justification is also wrong — since ib−oancf = ΔWC − dp, the "second leg" is −dp, not capx−dp, so this is not the decomposition it claims to be.

This is a standard industry z-score wrapper applied to the archive's existing best signal (AccrualsPerUnitRealCapitalFlow) — exactly the kind of cosmetic variant the objective warns against — and its stated motivation borrows a failure mode from a different signal (UnexpensedSoftAssetGrowth) whose diagnostic does not transfer to a parent that already delivers a −4.6 t-alpha.

A first difference of a bounded composition ratio is economically distinct from its level (surprise versus chronic state), the sign convention matches the expression, and the boundedness argument is correct, though the risk remains that the delta is mostly noise in a ratio whose denominator moves with the numerator.

Inventory growth as a return predictor is a well-documented published anomaly (Thomas–Zhang 2002; Belo–Lin 2012), and changing the deflator to capx+dp does not make it a new mechanism — it is a rediscovery dressed as a numerator-attribution experiment.

The book-tax verification story is interesting, but Δtxp is an order of magnitude smaller than total accruals for most firms, so this will be near-perfectly correlated with the archive's AccrualsPerUnitRealCapitalFlow while adding txp's missingness — an economically negligible perturbation of an existing signal rather than a genuine test of the tax channel.

A coherent and internally consistent stack of two independently validated archive components (cash-deterioration numerator × MIN-lag persistence) whose directional logic matches the negative expected sign, though it is incremental rather than novel and the two ingredients are likely far less orthogonal in practice than claimed, since both are driven by the same accrual level.

Replacing a one-year cash-flow delta with a three-year slope is dimensionally consistent (both are per-year changes) and the smoothing rationale is defensible, but this is close to a parameter tweak of the archive's leading signal rather than a distinct mechanism, and TREND over only three annual points is itself noisy.

The stock-versus-flow validation contrast is a genuinely distinct economic question and the sign logic is correct, but DELTA(che) is dominated by financing and investing activity rather than liquidity buffering, so the signal partly re-tests the external-financing conditioning that already failed in the archive (ExternallyFundedAccrualGrowth).

This is a minor decomposition of the archived WCAccrualPerRealCapitalFlow with the liability leg dropped, and the resulting numerator is essentially Sloan's current-operating-asset accrual component — a long-published decomposition rather than a cross-theme discovery.

This is a pure deflator swap on the leading signal, and the stated justification is internally inconsistent — gross PP&E is also small for asset-light firms (and missing more often), so it will not tame the tails but will instead tilt the sort toward a capital-intensity/industry sort that FF5 will not absorb.

A legitimate and previously untested temporal form (within-firm position rather than level or change) with a clear diagnostic payoff either way, but the reasoning contradicts itself — TS_RANK over five annual observations yields exactly the coarse five-point discreteness the companion proposal cites as the reason to avoid the persistence-count design — and the archive's weak change-based result (GrowthQualityDeterioration, t = −1.6) already hints that firm-relative deviations underperform the cross-sectional level.

This is a mechanical cross of two archive designs (TrendCashUnbackedAccruals × the MIN-with-lag persistence wrapper already tested on the delta version) whose likely outcome — slightly better alpha, diluted Fama-MacBeth slope — is already documented in the archive, making it a cosmetic recombination rather than a new mechanism.

Combining the flow-based cash trend and the stock-based cash-buffer drain into one deflated numerator is a defensible substantive extension with complementary archive evidence, though the hypothesis claims a conjunctive "fails both tests" reading that an additive numerator does not implement (a firm with a rising cash balance can offset a deteriorating trend), and DELTA(che) partially double-counts the che exclusion in the accrual proxy.

Changing the TREND window from 3 to 5 years on the archive's best existing signal is a pure parameter tweak of the kind the objective explicitly discourages, and it will mostly trade coverage and staleness against a nearly identical construct rather than test a distinct economic idea.

MAX(x, LAG(x)) on an already-tested ratio is close to a slowly-decaying smoothed version of the base signal and will be very highly correlated with TrendCashUnbackedAccruals, so the "asymmetry experiment" framing cannot rescue what is an operator flip with little independent information.

This is the only proposal that adds genuinely new information — a second moment of a bounded composition ratio rather than another transformation of its level — and is well scaled and clearly motivated, though it should be checked against known earnings/accrual-volatility quality measures and against a plausible confound with idiosyncratic volatility and size.

Adding (dp − capx) to the numerator makes the signal mechanically increasing in low capital spending while capex also sits in the deflator, so the term both double-counts the denominator and points against the well-documented investment anomaly (low investment firms earn higher returns), meaning a sign conflict is being asserted away rather than resolved.

This is a mechanical splice of two already-archived generation-5 variants (AgedCapitalSoftGrowth and SoftGrowthWithDepreciationRelief) whose stats are already nearly identical (fmb ≈ −4.3, ls_talpha ≈ −5.7/−6.3), so the combination is a cosmetic recombination almost certain to be collinear with both parents rather than a substantively different mechanism.

A clean, well-motivated attribution test that isolates one component of a composite, but it is close to the long-documented "change in depreciation rate / asset-life stretching" earnings-quality signal, and the archive's own InvestmentUnderSofteningDepreciation produced a *positive* alpha (t = +2.54) from the same depreciation-relief indicator, so the expected negative sign is not well supported by prior evidence.

Horizon of the accrual leg is a genuinely untested dimension in this archive and the construction is dimensionally coherent, but three-year cumulative accruals scaled by capital flow is uncomfortably close to the well-known net-operating-assets / long-horizon accrual bloat anomaly, so the incremental content over published work is limited and must be demonstrated rather than asserted.

This adds a single term (che) to the deflator of the archive's best-performing signal (TrendCashUnbackedAccruals) without changing the numerator or the economic claim being measured, making it a cosmetic scaling variant whose effect will largely be to tilt the ranking toward cash-poor, small, asset-heavy firms — i.e. a size/cash-holdings tilt rather than a new mechanism.

Internally inconsistent in magnitude: subtracting the three-year *level* of operating cash flow (typically far larger than the accrual term) rather than its change or slope means the expression is dominated by −MA(oancf)/(capx+dp), so this is effectively an inverted cash-flow-to-capital profitability signal — a known anomaly — not a test of accrual credibility.

The hypothesis speaks of a "count of levers pulled" but the expression sums dollar magnitudes, so a single large term dominates and the count interpretation fails; beyond that it is an explicitly alpha-maximizing stack of three already-tested terms, including DELTA(che), which the archive shows collapses the Fama-MacBeth slope (t = −1.51) while inflating portfolio alpha.

The stated mechanism is internally inconsistent — the reversible-asset-share moderator multiplies the *entire* ratio including the newly added depreciation-relief dollars, so plant-heavy (low act−che/at) firms are still shrunk toward zero rather than having their information "restored," making this a plain splice of two archive winners with a mis-specified rationale.

A legitimate amplify-versus-dilute test of the exposure channel, but it is fundamentally another deflator tweak on the same TrendCashUnbacked numerator already scaled by at, capx+dp, and capx+dp×(ppent/ppegt), so its incremental information is modest and it risks collapsing toward the already-tested at-scaled version.

Decomposing the best-slope moderator into its inventory component is a sensible and cheap diagnostic with a coherent markdown-risk story, though it is a single-component substitution rather than a new mechanism and inventory intensity is a well-worn conditioning variable.

Replacing the cash-flow *level* trend with a rate-times-stock change in cash return on installed capital is a genuinely different validation construct with a consistent sign (high accruals plus falling capital productivity → high signal → low returns), with the main risk being ppent-denominator instability for asset-light firms.

This is a rank-transform wrapper on an existing archive signal's moderator — a standard industry-neutralization robustness check rather than a substantively different economic mechanism, and the objective explicitly discourages cosmetic variants.

Targeting the archive's one genuine slope/alpha sign contradiction is worthwhile, but the fix only cleans the upper (acquisition step-up) tail while the sign conflict is at least as likely to originate in the lower tail, where ΔPPEGT−capx is driven by disposals and write-offs that the expression leaves untouched.

A coherent, sign-consistent stack of the archive's two strongest components (depreciation-relief numerator × strictly positive conversion-horizon moderator), but it is combinatorial rather than conceptually new, and the archive already shows this moderator trades alpha for slope, so the incremental information is modest.

Sign-coherent and defensible as an attribution test of whether the horizon moderator complements a stock rather than a flow numerator, but it is a near-duplicate of the preceding proposal differing only in the numerator's accumulation window, so at most one of the pair carries real information.

The high-water-mark drawdown is a genuinely new, non-negative validation construct that cannot offset the accrual term the way a signed trend can, the expression matches the hypothesis and the negative sign follows naturally; the main risk to check is that the drawdown term is mechanically correlated with cash-flow level and volatility and may be proxying for distressed low-profitability firms.

A legitimate and cleanly bounded ablation of the archive's best moderator, though the claim that it "strips out the exposed-asset numerator" is imprecise — replacing (act−che) with the capital-flow term changes both scale and economic content, so a null result would not cleanly establish that the exposed pool is essential.

Replacing the moderator with its monotone within-industry rank is a cosmetic transformation of SlowConversionSoftGrowth rather than a substantively different mechanism, and the stated economic claim ("ordinal risk classifier") is a post-hoc rationalization of a winsorization/scaling fix.

Internally inconsistent across the COALESCE branches — adding DELTA(lct−dlc) partially cancels the liability netting in the fallback working-capital branch while being a pure additive term in the ib−oancf branch, so the construct measures different things for different firms — and the positive loading on operating-liability growth runs against the accrual/net-operating-assets evidence that liability build-up is cash-generating, which the proposal does not confront.

This is a mechanical 2×2 cell-fill (archived depreciation-relief numerator × archived weak-cash weight), and since the weak-cash weight is algebraically the shared factor of the already-tested horizon weight (H = W·(act−che)/(capx+dp)), it adds attribution detail rather than a new economic mechanism.

Identical design move to the preceding proposal applied to a second archived numerator — the horizon-weighted cumulative bloat is already in the archive and the weak-cash weight is a strict component of that weight, so this cell is largely redundant both with the archive and with proposal 1 in the same batch.

An unweighted additive blend of two separately archived numerator terms is a defensible attribution test, but the non-negative, unbounded OCF-drawdown term is likely to dominate the accrual and depreciation dollars, so the resulting alpha risks being a repackaged cash-flow-shortfall/profitability signal rather than growth-composition information.

The trade-credit weight is economically distinct, but pairing it with an untested numerator confounds numerator and weight effects, and it is otherwise another cell in an increasingly exhaustive weight × numerator grid whose members differ only cosmetically.

The horizon weight has already been crossed with two numerators in the archive with near-identical results (alpha ≈ −0.053/−0.055, t ≈ −5.4/−5.6), so a third crossing is a cosmetic variant, and the stated "sign cancellation in the trend term" diagnosis is speculative given the trend-based version delivered essentially the same alpha.

This is the batch's only genuinely new construct — a high-water-mark drawdown in cash return on installed capital converted to dollars — and it cleanly discriminates cash-scale growth from productivity decay relative to the archived one-year productivity delta, though the ppent-scaled ratio will be noisy for asset-light firms and should be checked for coverage/tail instability.
